candidates.speaker: Dennis R. MacDonald
candidates.proposition: Paul and Josephus corroborate a mortal Jewish Jesus whose reinterpretation of Mosaic law continued among followers such as James.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person argument continues MacDonald’s identified presentation and is followed by his explicit transition to a second argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly supports historicity by connecting Q’s law-focused teacher with Pauline claims and an external account of James and his associates.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Carrier’s earlier position that Paul supplies no earthly biography and that no external evidence securely attests a historical Jesus.

candidates.contextSummary: MacDonald argues that Paul needed only Jesus’s crucifixion and legal significance for his theology, then interprets Josephus’s James passage as independent continuity with a Jewish law-reform movement.

candidates.speaker: Dennis R. MacDonald
candidates.proposition: Mark’s extensive epic mythologizing obscures historical information but makes best sense as the transformation of an earlier mortal Jewish teacher.
candidates.attributionBasis: MacDonald explicitly announces his second argument, maintains the floor throughout it, and addresses Carrier directly while granting part of Carrier’s account.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move turns agreed literary mimesis into a historicist explanation, distinguishing a mythologized person from a wholly invented revelatory figure.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Carrier’s use of Mark’s pervasive literary construction and dependence as support for doubting that an earthly Jesus preceded the Gospel narrative.

candidates.contextSummary: MacDonald concedes that Mark is historically unreliable and heavily shapes later Gospel tradition, but argues that Mark presents a baptized Galilean mortal whom God vindicates after death.

candidates.speaker: Dennis R. MacDonald
candidates.proposition: Early Johannine and Papian traditions preserve claims of personal witnesses and named disciples, supporting a historical Jesus despite later mythologization.
candidates.attributionBasis: MacDonald announces a final topic, reads and interprets the relevant traditions, and closes by explicitly summarizing the substance of his response to Richard.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument offers purported early witness transmission as an additional historicity route and identifies reconstructed Q as more valuable than Carrier’s Pauline reconstruction.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Carrier’s position that the surviving early sources do not provide reliable personal or independently transmitted knowledge of an earthly Jesus.

candidates.contextSummary: MacDonald treats First John’s collective witness claim and Papias’s preference for living voices as residual historical testimony while conceding that Johannine presentation strongly mythologizes Jesus.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: The reconstructed Q document is too insecure in existence, date, and contents to bear the historicist case assigned to it.
candidates.attributionBasis: The new turn directly addresses MacDonald’s preceding three points, uses first-person disagreement, and asks MacDonald a sustained counterfactual question about Q.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Because MacDonald identifies Q as his most important source, challenging its existence and reconstructive certainty attacks a principal foundation of his historicist inference.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: MacDonald’s reliance on reconstructed Q as the earliest and most valuable evidence for a mortal Jewish teacher who preceded Gospel mythmaking.

candidates.contextSummary: Carrier argues that Matthew–Luke overlap may have explanations without Q and asks whether disproving Q would remove nearly all of MacDonald’s affirmative historical evidence.

candidates.speaker: Dennis R. MacDonald
candidates.proposition: Even without Q, Matthew depends on earlier tradition portraying Jesus as an alternative Moses who authoritatively reinterpreted Jewish law.
candidates.attributionBasis: MacDonald accepts Carrier’s no-Q counterfactual for argument’s sake and develops a direct answer grounded in Matthew and form-critical oral tradition.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move supplies a fallback route for MacDonald’s historical-teacher thesis, preventing the affirmative case from depending entirely on the disputed Q hypothesis.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Carrier’s challenge that eliminating Q would also eliminate nearly all evidence supporting MacDonald’s reconstruction of a historical Jesus.

candidates.contextSummary: MacDonald grants Luke’s possible dependence on Matthew but contends that Matthew itself inherited an oral tradition assigning Jesus an alternative interpretation of Mosaic law.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: Portraying Jesus as a new Moses is equally explicable as literary construction from revealed, scriptural, or communal teachings and therefore does not establish historicity.
candidates.attributionBasis: Carrier explicitly rejects the asserted oral evidence, agrees with MacDonald’s literary observations, and then contrasts two explanations in a sustained response.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument accepts the observed Mosaic mimesis while denying its historicist force, presenting a revelatory-to-earthly construction that explains the same textual pattern.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: MacDonald’s claim that Matthew or Q inherited memories of a historical teacher whose distinctive program revised Mosaic law.

candidates.contextSummary: Carrier agrees that Matthew constructs Jesus through Deuteronomic and Mosaic models but argues that communities could place evolving revelations and scriptural teachings into an earthly character’s mouth.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: Mark can be understood as converting Pauline teachings about a preexistent revelatory Christ into an earthly prophetic narrative, leaving no evidence that distinguishes reification from memory.
candidates.attributionBasis: Carrier takes an explicitly marked turn, names his proposed direction of literary transformation, and sustains it until MacDonald begins a contrary evidential response.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the core mythicist mechanism by which an initially celestial Christ could acquire an earthly biography and explains why Gospel silence about Pauline cosmology is expected.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: MacDonald’s objection that the relevant tradition presents an earthly person rather than announcing teachings received through revelation from a preexistent being.

candidates.contextSummary: Carrier argues that Mark strips Pauline cosmology while narrativizing Pauline ideas, and maintains that the sources cannot decide whether Mosaic Jesus material reflects an actual teacher or later reification.

candidates.speaker: Dennis R. MacDonald
candidates.proposition: Multiple Pauline themes overlap with reconstructed Q, including sayings and the kingdom of God, making shared early tradition more plausible than wholesale Gospel invention from Paul.
candidates.attributionBasis: MacDonald explicitly denies that the parties lack evidence, enumerates Pauline–Q correspondences, and identifies the inference he draws from them before closing the point.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The correspondence argument is offered as positive evidence for continuity between Paul and an earlier Jesus tradition and against Carrier’s proposed direction from Paul into Mark.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Carrier’s claim that surviving evidence cannot distinguish memories of an actual teacher from later literary reification of revelatory or communal teachings.

candidates.contextSummary: MacDonald identifies overlapping mission, divorce, apostolic, return, and kingdom themes, interpreting them as Pauline–Q symbiosis while conceding that not every parallel is attributed to Jesus.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: Mythologization alone neither disproves nor proves existence, but its extent creates a need for independent evidence that Josephus’s James passage cannot securely provide.
candidates.attributionBasis: Carrier begins with an explicit statement of his published position and then directly answers MacDonald’s Josephus argument through cultic-brother and interpolation alternatives.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move states Carrier’s governing evidential standard and challenges the principal external attestation offered by MacDonald, preserving compatibility with nonexistence.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: MacDonald’s arguments that extensive fan-created mythology is compatible with a real person and that Josephus identifies James as Jesus’s biological brother.

candidates.contextSummary: Carrier grants that real people can be mythologized, but says independent confirmation is required and argues that Josephus may misunderstand a cultic title or contain a later Christian insertion.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: Paul’s failure to invoke the tax saying while arguing for taxation indicates that Mark later transformed Pauline instruction into a memorable earthly-Jesus episode.
candidates.attributionBasis: Carrier is invited by name to comment, explicitly resumes his earlier literary-direction argument, and presents a complete comparison between Romans and Mark.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The concrete comparison supplies affirmative evidence for Carrier’s proposed Paul-to-Mark direction rather than merely asserting that literary reification is abstractly possible.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: MacDonald’s judgment that deriving Gospel Jesus traditions from Paul is forced and that Pauline–Q overlap is better explained by shared earlier tradition.

candidates.contextSummary: Carrier reasons that Paul would likely have cited an authoritative Jesus saying when defending taxation, so its absence in Romans favors Mark’s later dramatization of Paul’s teaching.
